title: Family formation and child retention are becoming a metropolitan geography problem shaped by housing, care, schools and mobility
source_unit: Urban Institute research report, Where Do Families Live? Measuring Fertility and Child Migration Across Core Cities and Suburbs in the United States, June 25, 2026
geography: United States; 43 major metropolitan areas, comparing core cities, suburbs, exurbs and socioeconomic groups

observations.period: 2019-2023 ACS; family formation and child retention across metropolitan geographies

suburban_fertility.unit: general fertility rate in suburbs and exurbs, compared with 52 in core cities

suburban_child_retention.unit: child retention score in suburbs and exurbs, compared with 1.01 in core cities

geographic_variation.value: some core cities outperform suburbs on family outcomes

observations.method: Urban analysis of American Community Survey microdata at the Public Use Microdata Area level, using fertility, child-retention and child-population metrics across core and suburban geographies.
observations.uncertainty: The reported averages conceal substantial metro-level variation, and the study's regression relationships are controlled correlations rather than causal estimates.
observations.subgroup: Core-city, suburban and exurban residents across 43 major metropolitan areas.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher suburban rates do not mean families uniformly prefer suburbs; housing supply, selection, affordability, schools, commute patterns and migration constraints may jointly produce the observed distribution.

observations.period: 2019-2023 ACS; distinct local mechanisms for fertility and child retention

denominator.unit: major metropolitan areas with neighborhood and place-level covariates

family_sized_housing.value: strongly associated with retaining families with older children

child_care_density.value: strongly associated with retaining families with older children and more central to suburban family outcomes

young_adult_oriented_amenities.value: fertility is negatively associated with features such as bar density and influx of young adults

observations.method: Regression analysis pairing fertility and child-retention measures with housing, amenities, opportunity and neighborhood data.
observations.uncertainty: The publication identifies correlates, not intervention effects; amenity measures may also proxy for unobserved prices, household composition or labor-market sorting.
observations.subgroup: Families with children, childless couples, young adults and neighborhoods across core and suburban settings.
observations.counterinterpretation: Amenities associated with young adults may coexist with family-supportive resources; the negative association should not be read as a simple cultural conflict between generations.

observations.period: 2019-2023 ACS; different place-based conditions in core cities and suburbs

denominator.unit: primary metropolitan geography types compared by the study

core_city_conditions.value: education quality and commute patterns are more strongly linked to family outcomes in core cities

suburban_conditions.value: child-care availability plays a larger role in suburban family outcomes

college_educated_share.value: share of college-educated residents is negatively associated with fertility and retention in core cities but not suburbs

observations.method: Separate core-city and suburban comparisons using place-level covariates and regression analysis.
observations.uncertainty: These patterns do not identify whether education, commute, child care or resident composition is the operative mechanism; geographic categories also simplify heterogeneous neighborhoods.
observations.subgroup: Families and neighborhoods in core cities versus suburbs, with differences by education and labor-market context.
observations.counterinterpretation: A single family-friendly policy template may fail because the binding constraint differs by geography and life stage.

observations.period: 2019-2023 ACS; socioeconomic constraint and family-place choice

denominator.unit: high- and low-socioeconomic-status groups compared by the study

high_SES_response.value: high-SES families' location decisions are strongly shaped by housing, schools and amenities

low_SES_response.value: low-SES families show weaker responses to those local features

constraint_interpretation.value: the pattern suggests low-SES families have less ability to access family-friendly environments

observations.method: Socioeconomic-stratified analysis of family formation and child retention linked to neighborhood housing, education, care and opportunity conditions.
observations.uncertainty: Weaker observed responsiveness may reflect constrained choice, measurement limits, different preferences, or other unobserved barriers; it is not direct evidence of motivation or preference.
observations.subgroup: Higher- and lower-socioeconomic-status families across metropolitan neighborhoods.
observations.counterinterpretation: Improving amenities alone may not equalize family options if prices, credit, transportation, school access, discrimination or work schedules prevent households from reaching them.

boundary: This record treats fertility, child retention and family migration as linked to metropolitan housing, care, schooling, commute, amenities and socioeconomic constraint. It does not establish causal effects, define an ideal urban form, measure individual preferences, or imply that suburbanization alone explains demographic change.
